\chapter{The Other Five, and Where the Count Stops}
\label{ch:ja-native-count-six-to-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{17}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count things from one to ten in the native Japanese series, write the three further signs it cost, and say why the series stops at ten when the borrowed count does not.}

Run hitotsu to too in order, name the two numbers whose native word is used in both counts, and say what the two chapters cost in signs.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mu]{\ja{む} — three strokes, one of them a dot}

\label{lesson:JA-W17-mu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then one sign.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{five things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{five} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ね}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{む}} — \emph{mu}
\end{quote}

Three strokes, in this order, as KanjiVG records them: a horizontal across the upper left; then a long stroke from above it running down and looping at the foot; then a small separate mark up on the right.

That third mark is the one to watch. It is not attached to anything, and a \textbf{\ja{む}} without it is not a \textbf{\ja{む}}.

\textbf{\ja{ね}} also ends in a loop at the foot. The difference is what comes before it and that separate mark on the right.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Trace \textbf{\ja{む}} once, counting three lifts.
  \item Copy it; hide it; write it again.
  \item Check one thing: is the right-hand mark there, and separate?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes? (\textbf{Three.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke count and order per \href{https://kanjivg.tagaini.net/kanjivg/kanji/03080.html}{KanjiVG}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[muttsu]{\ja{むっつ} — six things}

\label{lesson:JA-C17-muttsu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then six.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{む}}, all three strokes — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{two} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{a little} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{むっつ}} — \emph{mu-t-tsu} — \textbf{six things}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ja{む}} from last lesson, then the small \textbf{\ja{っ}} and \textbf{\ja{つ}}.

Last chapter said of \textbf{\ja{ろく}}: \emph{six has one everyday reading; no native word stands beside it.} That was true of the borrowed count and it is worth putting straight now. The native word for six exists — it is \textbf{\ja{む}}, and you are holding it. What it does not do is stand inside the borrowed count the way \textbf{\ja{よん}} does.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{むっつ}}. Say \emph{roku} and \emph{muttsu}: same number, two words, no shared sound. Then run the count so far: \emph{hitotsu, futatsu, mittsu, yottsu, itsutsu, muttsu}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do \textbf{\ja{ろく}} and \textbf{\ja{むっつ}} share a sound? (\textbf{No.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E5\%85\%AD\%E3\%81\%A4}{Wiktionary: muttsu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nanatsu]{\ja{ななつ} — seven things, and the seam again}

\label{lesson:JA-C17-nanatsu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then seven.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{six things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{three} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{し}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ななつ}} — \emph{na-na-tsu} — \textbf{seven things}
\end{quote}

No new sign, and no new word either — you have said \textbf{\ja{なな}} since the last chapter.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — the second place the seam shows}]
\textbf{\ja{なな}} is the native word, and the borrowed count uses it — the same move you saw at four with \textbf{\ja{よん}}. Write the two rows out and the pattern is exact:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the reading} & \textbf{four} & \textbf{seven} \\
\midrule
borrowed reading & \emph{shi} & \emph{shichi} \\
native word, used instead & \textbf{\ja{よん}} & \textbf{\ja{なな}} \\
native count & \textbf{\ja{よっつ}} & \textbf{\ja{ななつ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two places in ten where the native word walked into the borrowed count and stayed, and both of them are places where the borrowed reading collides with another word. This is the seam, and you have now seen both ends of it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{ななつ}}. Say \emph{nana}, then \emph{nanatsu}: the same word, once as a number and once as a count of things.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word did this lesson cost you? (\textbf{None} — you already had \textbf{\ja{なな}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E4\%B8\%83\%E3\%81\%A4}{Wiktionary: nanatsu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ya]{\ja{や} — the long stroke goes first}

\label{lesson:JA-W17-ya}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then one sign.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{seven things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{four}, and which of its two readings is the native one — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{slowly} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{や}} — \emph{ya}
\end{quote}

Three strokes, and the order is the surprise. KanjiVG has them as: \textbf{first} the long sweep, starting low on the left and running up and away to the right; \textbf{then} a short tick at the top; \textbf{then} the long stroke that comes down through the middle and out to the bottom right.

Look at the finished shape and you would guess the descender was drawn first. It is not. Draw the sweep, then the tick, then the descender.

\textbf{\ja{よ}} is already yours and shares the same first sound. It is built the other way round — the crossing stroke comes down first there.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Trace \textbf{\ja{や}} in the KanjiVG order, saying \textquotedblleft{}sweep, tick, down\textquotedblright{}.
  \item Copy it; hide it; write it again.
  \item Write \textbf{\ja{よ}} beside it and say both.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which stroke is first? (\textbf{The sweep.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke count and order per \href{https://kanjivg.tagaini.net/kanjivg/kanji/03084.html}{KanjiVG}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yattsu]{\ja{やっつ} — eight things}

\label{lesson:JA-C17-yattsu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then eight.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{や}}, sweep first — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{four} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ゆ}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{やっつ}} — \emph{ya-t-tsu} — \textbf{eight things}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ja{や}} from last lesson, the small \textbf{\ja{っ}}, and \textbf{\ja{つ}}.

Eight is the plain case. \textbf{\ja{はち}} is the borrowed word, \textbf{\ja{やっつ}} is the native one, neither has walked into the other's count, and there is nothing to disentangle. The last chapter used \textbf{\ja{はち}} for exactly the same job — to show what the ordinary case looks like once the odd ones have been seen.

Say the run: \emph{hitotsu, futatsu, mittsu, yottsu, itsutsu, muttsu, nanatsu, yattsu.} Eight of ten, and two signs left to buy.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{やっつ}}. Say \emph{hachi}, then \emph{yattsu}. Then run the eight in order without stopping.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is eight one of the crossing places? (\textbf{No.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E5\%85\%AB\%E3\%81\%A4}{Wiktionary: yattsu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[no]{\ja{の} — one stroke, and the last sign of the chapter}

\label{lesson:JA-W17-no}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the fifth and last sign.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eight things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{seven} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{please say it} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{の}} — \emph{no}
\end{quote}

One stroke. KanjiVG's data holds a single path: start high and to the right of centre, run down and left, round the bottom, up the left side and across the top, finishing by crossing what you have just drawn.

\textbf{\ja{ひ}}, from the start of this chapter, was also one stroke and never closed. \textbf{\ja{の}} closes and then keeps going.

This is the fifth sign this chapter has bought, and the last. Everything after it is words.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Trace \textbf{\ja{の}} once without lifting.
  \item Copy it; hide it; write it again.
  \item Write \textbf{\ja{ひ}} and \textbf{\ja{の}} side by side: one stroke each, one open, one crossed.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many signs has this chapter bought? (\textbf{Five}, and this is the last.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke count and order per \href{https://kanjivg.tagaini.net/kanjivg/kanji/0306e.html}{KanjiVG}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kokonotsu]{\ja{ここのつ} — nine things}

\label{lesson:JA-C17-kokonotsu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the longest word in the chapter.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{の}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nine} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{here} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ここのつ}} — \emph{ko-ko-no-tsu} — \textbf{nine things}
\end{quote}

Four beats, four signs, and only \textbf{\ja{の}} is new — you bought it last lesson.

Read the first two signs on their own: \textbf{\ja{ここ}}, the word for \emph{here} you have had since chapter ten. \textbf{They are the same two signs, and it means nothing.} \emph{kokono-} is simply the native word for nine; it is not built on \emph{here} and there is no story joining them. Say so and move on — an accident that gets explained is worse than one that gets named.

What it does mean is that you can write this four-beat word straight away, which no other word in the chapter has managed.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{ここのつ}}. Say \emph{hachi}, \emph{ku}, then \emph{yattsu}, \emph{kokonotsu} — both counts, two numbers each. Then say \emph{ku} and \emph{kokonotsu} again. Then say \emph{koko} and \emph{kokonotsu} and remind yourself that the second is not made of the first.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many beats? (\textbf{Four.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E4\%B9\%9D\%E3\%81\%A4}{Wiktionary: kokonotsu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tō]{\ja{とお} — ten things, and the end of the run}

\label{lesson:JA-C17-too}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the last word.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nine things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ten}, then \emph{twenty-five} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{a little more} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{とお}} — \emph{tō} — \textbf{ten things}
\end{quote}

Two signs, both old, and \textbf{no \ja{つ} at all}.

Nine words in this count carry the \textbf{\ja{つ}} that does the counting. The tenth drops it, and that is not a spelling quirk — it is the edge of the count. \textbf{\ja{とお}} is where the native series ends. There is no \emph{eleven things} in it.

Above ten, Japanese has only the borrowed count and a counter word, which is exactly the machinery the next chapter is for. \textbf{\ja{じゅう}} goes on to ninety-nine; \textbf{\ja{とお}} goes nowhere.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{とお}}. Say \emph{juu}, then \emph{tō}: same number, and only one of them can be built on. Then say \emph{kokonotsu, tō} and stop.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Can you say \emph{eleven things} this way? (\textbf{No.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E5\%8D\%81}{Wiktionary: too}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{The other ten, in order at last}

\label{lesson:JA-R17-the-other-ten}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ten things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{one thing} — \textbf{R2}, thirteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{I understood} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{here} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Nothing new arrives here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — the run}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the borrowed ten, then the native ten, back to back
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ku}, then \emph{kokonotsu} — the two nines, one from each count
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ja{ろ}} from last chapter, then \textbf{\ja{ひ}}, \textbf{\ja{ふ}}, \textbf{\ja{む}}, \textbf{\ja{や}}, \textbf{\ja{の}} — the one sign the borrowed count bought late, and the five this chapter bought
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
Ten words, and \textbf{five signs}: \textbf{\ja{ひ}}, \textbf{\ja{ふ}}, \textbf{\ja{む}}, \textbf{\ja{や}}, \textbf{\ja{の}}. Five of the ten words cost nothing at all — \textbf{\ja{みっつ}}, \textbf{\ja{よっつ}}, \textbf{\ja{いつつ}}, \textbf{\ja{ななつ}} and \textbf{\ja{とお}} were spelled entirely out of signs you already had.

Two things about the shape of what you now hold:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item The native count \textbf{stops at ten}. \textbf{\ja{とお}} carries no \textbf{\ja{つ}} and nothing is built on it. The borrowed count runs to ninety-nine on \textbf{\ja{じゅう}} alone.
  \item At \textbf{four} and \textbf{seven} the native word is the one used in \emph{both} counts. Nowhere else.
\end{itemize}

What the chapter has not yet said is what \textbf{\ja{つ}} actually is. It is not a decoration and it is not part of the words: it is a \textbf{counter}, and the next chapter is about choosing one.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many signs did the chapter cost? (\textbf{Five}.) Where does the native count stop? (\textbf{At \ja{とお}}.) Which two numbers use the native word in both counts? (\textbf{Four and seven}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
